catalog_quote: Details of the stress patterns of Jaminjung and Ngaliwurru are unclear at present. Primary word stress generally falls on the first syllable of a phonological word. However, in forms longer than two syllables, heavy syllables may attract stress when they are in non-initial position. In canonical complex verbs, main stress falls on the coverb, at least when it precedes the verb; the verb receives secondary stress. This stress pattern can serve to distinguish coverb – verb combinations from the combination of an adverbial nominal with a verb (see also §2.2.2.4, §3.2).
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Jaminjung-Ngaliwurru is not in the catalog. The two title-keyword items are both by the language's main documenters but neither is about word stress: Schultze-Berndt & Simard 2012 (Linguistics 50(5)) concerns prosodic phrasing and information structure in discontinuous NPs, and Simard 2013 (SOAS WPL 16) concerns the intonation-unit-level 'iconic lengthening' construction (as described first-hand in Simard 2010 ch. 5). Neither could be opened by automated download: the 2012 paper's green-OA repository copies (Manchester Pure post-peer-review PDF; SOAS Research Online CC-BY) sit behind an automated-access block challenges, the De Gruyter page returns an empty 202, and no copy of the 2013 paper was located (old SOAS pages 404, the Internet Archive offline, not on HAL; Both get low acquisition priority. The best first-hand statements were already held by the project and were read and verified in this search of works with stress in the title: Schultze-Berndt 2000:42 sec. 2.1.4 (primary stress generally on the first syllable of the phonological word; non-initial heavy syllables may attract stress in longer words; coverb carries main stress in complex verbs; details 'unclear at present'; quote verified against the rendered scan page) and Simard 2010:112-113, 166 (perceived initial stress on content words, stem-initial in prefixed verbs; acoustically cued by duration and intensity, domain = prosodic word). No catalog record exists to confirm or supersede; under records the attempted downloads and the saved page image.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress on the first syllable of the phonological word (impressionistic); in words of three or more syllables a non-initial heavy (closed) syllable may attract stress; author flags the details as unclear. Corroborated by Simard 2010 (pp.111-113): stress perceived on the first syllable of content words, trochaic pattern; in prefixed inflected verbs main stress may fall on the first syllable of the stem rather than on the word-initial bound-pronoun prefix.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Schultze-Berndt: in coverb+verb complex predicates the inflecting verb carries secondary stress, main stress on the coverb. Simard 2010: 'some variation as to the allocation of the secondary stress', pattern assumed trochaic; some suffixes (up to 3 syllables) may receive at least secondary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Heavy syllables in non-initial position may attract stress in words longer than two syllables (Schultze-Berndt); in inflected verbs stress may fall on the stem-initial syllable after the pronominal prefix rather than word-initially (Simard 2010: 113-114). Simard's acoustic study (sec. 3.3.4) finds the initial pitch movement is pitch reset rather than a stress target; likely stress cues are duration and intensity, correlates not yet established.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain stated as the phonological word; Simard's acoustic results also point to the word (not the phrasal constituent) as the stress domain. Both descriptions are impressionistic for stress placement; statement covers both Jaminjung and Ngaliwurru.
new_statements.identity_note: Schultze-Berndt 2000 explicitly covers both Jaminjung and the Ngaliwurru dialect (Glottolog treats them as one language, djam1255; dialects jami1236 Jaminjung / ngal1293 Ngaliwurru); the stress statement is made for 'Jaminjung and Ngaliwurru' jointly. Simard 2010 describes Jaminjung (speakers from Timber Creek/Kununurra area, some also Ngaliwurru speakers).

new_statements.reading: Primary stress is word-initial on the phonological word (hedged as 'generally'), with a possible weight-sensitive exception: in words of three or more syllables a non-initial heavy syllable may attract stress. Within complex predicates the coverb carries main stress and the inflected verb secondary stress. The author explicitly flags the system as under-described. Corroborated independently by Simard 2010:112-113 and 166 (perceived initial stress on content words; in inflected verbs stress may sit on the stem-initial syllable after the pronominal prefix; acoustic cues = duration and intensity, domain = prosodic word). Together these support an initial-stress coding with a weight-sensitivity caveat and a prefix-skipping caveat for verbs.

sources.citation: Simard, Candide. 2010. The Prosodic Contours of Jaminjung, a Language of Northern Australia. PhD thesis, University of Manchester.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: Stress is perceived on the first syllable of content words, another widespread pattern in Australian languages. In inflected verb forms, the main stress may be heard not on the word-initial syllable, which is the bound pronoun, but on the first syllable of the stem. [...] As to stress, the results suggest that its domain is the word, rather than the phrasal constituents, and that its most likely cues are a longer duration and higher intensity. Further research would be needed to establish its exact correlates.
sources.locator: pp. 112-113 (sec. 3.2.2.4 and 3.2.2.5 Summary); acoustic result p. 166 and ch. 6 conclusion
sources.note: Sec. 3.2.2.4 Stress, pp.111-113 (impressionistic): stress heard on first syllables, trochaic, variation in secondary stress; each nominal stem, verb form and coverb gets at least one stress; some suffixes may take (secondary) stress; in inflected verbs main stress may fall on first syllable of the stem rather than the pronominal prefix. Sec. 3.3.4 (acoustic): initial pitch movement reflects pitch reset, stress domain is the word, likely cues longer duration and higher intensity; exact correlates need further research.

sources.note: Not read; no open copy located (old soas.ac. The topic is the 'iconic lengthening' construction described first-hand in Simard 2010 ch. 5 (pp. 315-316, 344): 'Lengthening is a device used in Jaminjung by which the durational aspect of an action is iconically represented by lengthening the vowel in the coverb or verb in the first IU' -- an intonation-unit-level expressive/durational phenomenon, not word-stress placement.
